e.etymology: A Spanish-spelled form of Julissa, a 20th-century blend built on Julia that spread through Latin America; the Y follows the way the name is said.
An English surname from Old French engaine, ingenuity or trickery, a nickname for a clever person. It has been an occasional American first name since the 1800s.
A spelling of Jaheim, which entered US use in 2001 and 2002 with the R&B singer Jaheim.
An African-American coinage that joins the Ja- prefix to Kiya or Kia; it is also close to Zakiya, the Arabic name meaning pure.

e.meaning: renowned ruler; later read as ruler of the world
e.etymology: The Spanish spelling of Vladimir, written as it sounds in Spanish, where b and v are said alike. Vladimir joins Slavic vlad, rule, to a second part meaning great, later taken as mir, peace or world.
Sanskrit megha, cloud, the rain cloud of the monsoon.
A modern American name that reads as a feminine form of Jalen or as Ja- plus Lena; it is also close to Jelena, the South Slavic form of Helen.
From Old High German gund, battle, and heri, army. Gunther is the Burgundian king of the Nibelungenlied; Americans know the name from the coffee-shop manager on Friends.

assoc.t: Gunther, the Central Perk manager on Friends

e.etymology: A respelling of Chloe, from Greek khloe, a young green shoot, a title of the goddess Demeter. The Kh- follows Khloé Kardashian.

assoc.t: Khloé Kardashian, reality TV star, same sound

e.etymology: A respelling of Erica, the feminine of Eric, from Old Norse Eirikr, ever ruler, written with the Aa- of Aaron.
An African-American coinage that joins the Da- prefix to Miya or Mia; also spelled Damiyah.

e.meaning: first ray of the sun, dawn
e.etymology: A modern Indian name from Sanskrit arushi, the reddish one, a Vedic word for the dawn; it is usually glossed as first ray of the sun.
The Spanish and Scandinavian spelling of Ruth, the biblical Moabite woman loyal to Naomi, whose Hebrew name is usually read as friend or companion.
e.note: In English a rut is a groove or a dull routine, and the rut is the mating season of deer.

assoc.t: rut, a groove or dull routine; the mating season of deer

e.etymology: A modern name that reads as Riley or Bailey with a Rae- start; Railey also exists as an English surname.
The Hebrew pet form of Yonatan (Jonathan), God has given; the Israeli equivalent of Johnny.
e.note: Yoni is also the Sanskrit word for the vulva or womb, familiar from yoga and wellness writing.

e.etymology: Arabic qasim, one who divides or distributes. Qasim was a son of the Prophet Muhammad, who is known as Abu al-Qasim.
Most US use is as a variant of Orion, the hunter of Greek myth and the constellation named for him; the origin of that name is unknown. Orian is also a modern Israeli name.
Arabic talal, from the root t-l-l, dew or fine rain. It was the name of King Talal of Jordan.
Emma and Grace written as one name. Emma is Germanic for whole or universal; Grace is the virtue name from Latin gratia.
Igbo ike, strength or power, and nna, father. The father may be the child's own or God.
From Sanskrit tejas, fiery energy, splendor or brilliance; in Hindi and Punjabi tej also means sharp and swift.

e.meaning: famous spear (from a pet form of Roger)
e.etymology: An English surname from Dogge, a medieval pet form of Roger, a Germanic name made of words for fame and spear. As a first name it is rare and mostly American.

assoc.t: Dodge, the American car and truck brand
Dodge City, the Kansas cattle town of Wild West fame

e.meaning: great house, the title of Egypt's kings
e.etymology: A common respelling of Pharaoh, the title of the kings of ancient Egypt, from Egyptian per-aa, great house. Jazz saxophonist Pharoah Sanders and the racehorse American Pharoah both used this spelling.
e.note: This is a nonstandard spelling of the word pharaoh, so expect it to be corrected.

e.etymology: A modern blend of Mattie with the -lyn ending, also read as a spelling of Madilyn.
The English word, from Old English regnboga, rain bow. As a given name it dates from the counterculture of the 1970s.

e.meaning: short form of Cornelia, Antonela and similar names
e.etymology: A short form of names ending in -nela or -nelia, such as Kornélia, Petronela and Antonela, popular in the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Poland; in Spain it also shortens Manuela.
A modern American coinage that puts Em-, as in Emma and Emily, on the -iyah ending of Aaliyah and Amiyah.
The Spanish form of Stuart, the Scottish royal surname, from Old English stigweard, steward. It is especially common in Guatemala.
Mostly a spelling of Kade or Cade, an English surname from an Old English byname meaning round or from a word for a cask. Kaid is also a transliteration of Arabic qaid, leader or commander.
A spelling of Jayceon, the elaboration of Jason and Jace known from rapper The Game, born Jayceon Taylor.
Yiddish blum, flower, from the same Germanic root as English bloom. It was brought to the US by Jewish immigrants around 1900 and remains in use in Hasidic families.
The Dutch and Afrikaans spelling of Elise, a short form of Elisabeth, from Hebrew Elisheva, my God is an oath.
